title: Saadia Gaon
hookLine: a Gaon translates the Torah into Arabic and writes on faith and reason

cards: Believers whose belief is clouded. Doubters who are proud of doubting. And thoughtful people sinking, as he puts it, in a sea of confusion, with no one to pull them out.
That's what one author sees when he looks around, and it worries him enough to write. Not a sermon: an argument, step by step, using reason, about what can be known and how.

The author is Saadia, head of the academy at Sura. He's a Gaon, like the ones we met this week, but his questions aren't about one case of law. They're about whether faith and thinking can stand on the same ground.

teach.b: Saadia did two big things. First, he translated the Torah into Arabic, the everyday language of the Jews around him, and it has come down to us in Hebrew letters.
It's often called his Tafsir, an Arabic word for explanation, because his translation explains as it goes.

teach.h: THE BOOK OF BELIEFS AND OPINIONS.
teach.b: Second, he wrote the book from the hook, known in English as The Book of Beliefs and Opinions.

In it he lays out how a person comes to know things: what the senses observe, what reason grasps, what you can necessarily infer, and reliable tradition, which for him includes the Torah. Here's his bold claim.
Faith and reason don't compete. Rightly used, they lead to the same truth. Then he asks the obvious question back.
If reason can reach it, why does anyone need revelation? His answer, in plain words: because thinking things through takes a long time, and some people never get there.
Revelation gives the truth to everyone at once, the young and the busy included. Reason lets you understand it, test it, and defend it when someone challenges you. Not one instead of the other.
His translation brought the Torah into the language of the street; his philosophy brought the street's hardest questions into the Torah.

how: Saadia's Arabic translation of the Torah is still read in some Yemenite Jewish communities alongside the Hebrew, and his Book of Beliefs and Opinions is studied in courses on Jewish thought.

games.q: you're Saadia. a student asks: if reason can reach the truth, why do we need revelation at all? what do you answer?
o: revelation gives the truth to everyone at once; reason helps us understand and defend it.
reason can't be trusted at all.
games.why: Saadia's answer: reasoning takes long and some never finish, so revelation reaches everyone, and reason lets you understand and defend it.

practice: Here's a verse from the Psalms, in the 1917 Jewish translation: "Thy word is a lamp unto my feet, And a light unto my path."
Say it slowly in your head, then put it into the words you actually use, as if to someone who has never heard it, and try another version, noticing what gets lost and what gets clearer.
If you pray, you can end by saying the verse as it is written.
